To "play devil's advocate" means to argue for a side you don't personally believe in, just to test an idea, challenge a viewpoint, or push a discussion further. The person doing it is not genuinely opposing you — they are deliberately taking the opposite side as a mental exercise, to make the conversation stronger and more well-rounded.

Think of it as stress-testing an idea. Like a bridge engineer who deliberately puts extra weight on a bridge — not because they want it to fall, but because they want to be sure it won't.

This idiom has a fascinating and very specific origin — the Catholic Church.

When the Church considered making someone a saint (a process called "canonization"), it was an extremely serious and rigorous affair. They couldn't just declare someone a saint because people liked them. They needed proof — verified miracles, a life of genuine virtue, and so on.

To make sure the process was fair and thorough, the Church assigned a special official role called the "Advocatus Diaboli" — Latin for "Devil's Advocate." This person's job was to argue against the candidate for sainthood. They would dig up flaws, question the so-called miracles, challenge the evidence, and raise every possible doubt.

Here's the crucial point: the Devil's Advocate didn't actually believe the candidate was unworthy. Their job was simply to represent the skeptical side — to argue the "devil's" case — so that only truly deserving people made it through. This role was formally introduced around 1587 under Pope Sixtus V.

The opposite role was called the "Advocatus Dei" — the "God's Advocate" (or "Promoter of the Cause") — who argued in favor of the candidate.

Pope John Paul II abolished this formal role in 1983, which is one reason the Church has canonized saints more quickly in recent decades. But the phrase "devil's advocate" lived on and entered everyday language.

Today, the phrase has no religious meaning at all. It simply means: "I'm going to argue the other side — not because I believe it, but to examine this more carefully."

It is almost always used to:

1. Test the strength of an idea. If your argument can withstand a devil's advocate challenge, it's probably solid. If it falls apart, you know you need to rethink it.

2. Spark deeper discussion. Sometimes conversations go stale because everyone agrees too quickly. Playing devil's advocate forces people to defend their views and think harder.

3. Find weaknesses before they become real problems. In business, planning, or strategy, someone playing devil's advocate can spot flaws early — before they cause damage.

4. Stay intellectually honest. It prevents "groupthink," which is when a group of people all agree without anyone stopping to question whether they're actually right.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The phrase is almost always introduced with "to play devil's advocate" or "let me play devil's advocate." This is the speaker's way of warning you: "What I'm about to say is not my real opinion — I'm just exploring the other side."

Here are some natural examples:

  • "I love your idea for the startup. But just to play devil's advocate — what if customers aren't willing to pay that price?"
  • "She played devil's advocate during the meeting, raising concerns about the budget even though she fully supported the project."
  • "Let me be devil's advocate here: what if we're wrong about this?"
  • "He doesn't actually disagree with us — he's just playing devil's advocate to make sure we've thought everything through."

Sometimes people use "playing devil's advocate" as a social shield — a polite way to introduce an opinion they actually hold but are hesitant to say directly, because it might seem controversial or unpopular. By framing it as "just playing devil's advocate," they soften the delivery and reduce the risk of conflict.

So in real life, when someone says "let me play devil's advocate," it could mean one of two things:

  • They genuinely don't believe what they're about to say, but want to explore it. (The traditional, correct use.)
  • They actually do believe it, but they're using the phrase to cushion it. (A common but softer use.)

Context usually tells you which one it is.
Is It a Positive or Negative Thing?

Mostly positive. Playing devil's advocate is seen as a sign of critical thinking, intellectual honesty, and genuine helpfulness. A good devil's advocate makes ideas better.

However, it can become annoying or unproductive if someone constantly argues the opposite side without ever being constructive — using it as an excuse to be difficult rather than to genuinely help. The goal of a devil's advocate should always be to improve the thinking, not just to obstruct it.

The next time someone says "let me play devil's advocate," you'll know they're not being your enemy — they're being your editor.
